entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The German Federal Bank, known as Deutsche Bundesbank, was established in 1957 as the central bank of the Federal Republic of Germany, situated in Frankfurt am Main. This institution plays a pivotal role in the European monetary framework, influencing both national and European economic policies. As a successor to the Bank deutscher Länder, the Bundesbank emerged in a post-World War II context, where it was instrumental in stabilizing the West German economy and supporting the rapid economic growth known as the "Wirtschaftswunder" or economic miracle.

The Bundesbank's mandate includes maintaining price stability and overseeing monetary policy within Germany. It became a key player in the creation of the European Monetary Union and the euro currency, which were formalized in the 1990s. The bank's policies and practices set the standard for monetary governance in Europe, particularly through its focus on inflation targeting and fiscal discipline. The Bundesbank's independence from political influence has been vital in establishing credibility and trust in its monetary policy.

The legacy of the Bundesbank is profound, as it laid the groundwork for the European Central Bank (ECB), which formally took over many of its responsibilities in 1998. The Bundesbank model of central banking has inspired numerous countries and institutions worldwide, reinforcing the importance of independence in monetary policy to achieve macroeconomic stability. In the broader scope of European integration, the Bundesbank has been a cornerstone in the establishment of a unified monetary policy, shaping the economic landscape of the Eurozone.
